𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐰𝐞𝐫 𝐢𝐬 𝐢𝐧.
Many of you correctly identified the graph as the relationship between firing temperature and NOₓ and CO emissions in a gas turbine combustor.

At first glance, it illustrates a well-known combustion trade-off:
📈 As firing temperature increases, NOₓ emissions tend to rise.
📉 At the same time, CO emissions decrease as combustion becomes more complete.

But this graph is about much more than emissions. For decades, gas turbine manufacturers have pushed firing temperatures higher because they unlock higher efficiency, higher specific power output, and better combined-cycle performance.

The challenge is that every increase in firing temperature comes with consequences:
• Higher NOₓ formation
• Increased cooling requirements
• More compressor bleed air diverted to protect combustor and turbine hot-section components
• Greater demands on materials and cooling technologies

In other words, achieving higher firing temperatures is not just a combustion challenge, it's a balancing act between performance, emissions, cooling, and durability.

The answer matters because the best turbine configuration is not decided only by full-load efficiency. It is also shaped by how the plant is expected to operate across the load range.

When load decreases, an 
话题标签
#OCGT typically sees a sharper drop in efficiency. In simple-cycle operation, more of the fuel energy leaves as hot exhaust, and that energy is not recovered for additional power generation.

A 
话题标签
#CCGT behaves differently. The gas turbine exhaust is sent to the HRSG, where it produces steam that drives a steam turbine, so part of the energy that would otherwise be lost is still converted into useful electrical output.

That is why the CCGT efficiency curve is usually flatter than the OCGT curve at part load. The combined-cycle arrangement helps reduce the efficiency penalty that is much more visible in simple-cycle operation.

But there is also a trade-off. CCGTs usually do not offer the same turndown range, startup speed, or operating flexibility as OCGTs because the steam cycle adds thermal inertia and extra constraints during transients.

So the real question is not only which technology is more efficient.
It is which technology best matches the plant’s expected operating profile:
🔹OCGT for fast starts, peaking duty, and higher flexibility.
🔹CCGT for stronger efficiency, especially when the plant will spend significant time at part load.

In other words, technology selection should also answer this question:
𝐖𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐞 𝐰𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐩𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐭 𝐬𝐩𝐞𝐧𝐝 𝐦𝐨𝐬𝐭 𝐨𝐟 𝐢𝐭𝐬 𝐥𝐢𝐟𝐞 𝐨𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐥𝐨𝐚𝐝 𝐜𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞?

The best operators do not upgrade everything at once. They sequence investments based on operational pain points, outage windows, remaining life, and dispatch strategy.

This 4-wave upgrade funnel shows how modernization priorities typically evolve:
🔹 Wave 1 — Controls and reliability upgrades. Focus on trips, failed starts, sensors, valves, actuation, and flame detection.
🔹 Wave 2 — Airflow and combustion optimization. Target ambient penalties, combustion instability, turndown, emissions, and efficiency.
🔹 Wave 3 — Compressor and hot-gas-path upgrades. Improve output, heat rate, coatings, and interval extension during major outages.
🔹 Wave 4 — Rotor strategy. Address life extension, operational life recovery, refurbished rotors, or rotor exchange.

The key principle: 👉 Upgrade sequencing should follow operational bottlenecks and asset economics, not trends.

A unit with strong dispatch value and long-term strategic importance can justify deeper investment.
But many plants can unlock significant value simply by stabilising controls and improving operability first.

The themes that emerged reflected the breadth of aspirations, opportunities and realities that shape women's careers today. These will continue to steer Women@BCG's focus areas as we create more pathways for our women employees to learn, connect and thrive at every stage of their careers.

Today, the future of ultra-long-haul travel became a reality.

An Airbus A350-1000ULR powered by our Trent XWB-97 engines completed a non-stop journey from Australia to Europe in 24 hours and 24 minutes, as part of Qantas' Project Sunrise programme.

A flight of this scale demands exceptional performance. With more than 4.5 million flying hours in service, the Trent XWB-97 combines proven reliability, durability and efficiency to give airlines the confidence to connect the world's most distant cities.

As the aircraft crossed Europe, it passed over Derby, the home of the engines that made the journey possible and the place where Rolls-Royce has been helping shape the future of flight for more than a century.

Project Sunrise is a powerful example of what can be achieved through innovation, partnership and a shared ambition to push the boundaries of aviation.

Congratulations to everyone involved.

Boards and CEOs rarely disagree on the urgency of AI. Where they often diverge is on speed, scale, and how much measurable business impact to expect.

Asuka Hayashi, Partner in our Tokyo office, shares her perspective on surfacing Japan's innovation potential for a global audience. *Japanese follows English. 

I have been working on a project to identify and map innovation across Japan, making it accessible to global experts who have historically found it difficult to navigate due to language and other barriers. 

One of the most meaningful aspects of this work was using AI to conduct research that would have taken months manually. AI made it possible to go both broad and deep, and to do so in a fraction of the time. Distilling all of that into something concise and immediately actionable for busy global experts was equally important, and one of the most engaging parts of the work. 

Before my career at BCG, I was a researcher myself. Being able to shine a light on Japan's research and innovation capabilities, and share that with the world, is something I find deeply rewarding.

Referrals may be one of the most overlooked sources of profitable growth. An analysis of more than 10 million consumers found that referred customers make up about 20% of new customers but generate 72% of the profits from that group. They cost less to acquire, stay longer, spend more, and often bring in other high-value customers.

Yet many attribution systems still overvalue paid channels while missing the impact of word of mouth. Leading companies track referral behavior, identify genuine promoters, and create experiences people want to recommend.

Southeast Asia is set to drive more than 25% of global energy demand growth through 2035, yet much of the region still relies on volatile fossil fuel imports to meet it.

In a recent op-ed for The Edge Singapore, BCG’s Marko Lackovic argues that the Asean Power Grid has shifted from a long-standing ambition to an urgent strategic necessity, and that Singapore sits at the center of this shift.

Energy security and energy sovereignty don't have to be competing goals. Singapore's plan to import 6GW of low-carbon electricity by 2035, worth roughly 30% of its projected supply, shows how a well-designed regional grid can deliver affordability, reliability, and resilience together. Getting there will take sustained investment in domestic transmission and clear, bankable rules for cross-border trade.
